<reason>Side A (CON) won a close debate on disciplined burden enforcement. A's central demand—that PRO show benefits exceeding full lifetime cost against competing uses of a national budget—was never squarely answered. When A's pressure question forced B to name a rejection condition, B restricted the comparison to "the same communities," and A's Rebuttal 2 exposed exactly why that boundary was arbitrary; B never repaired it in closing. B also twice mischaracterized A's position, claiming A conceded a "permanent" gap after A2.1 explicitly denied permanence, and asserting A "refused to name any metric" before A had even spoken. B's rhetoric was superior ("find out by building," "commercial viability wearing a disguise") and the falsifiability-asymmetry move was genuinely clever, and B did adapt honestly in closing by accepting A's metric. But the rhetorical edge rests partly on misdescription, while A answered pressure questions more concretely, kept a consistent standard from opening to close, and left the opportunity-cost clash live and unresolved. B's hollowing-out counterfactual and electrification analogy gave PRO real substance, keeping this competitive rather than clean.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 2 (A4.5) exposing the "same communities" restriction in B's falsification test: a national subsidy draws on a national budget, so excluding greater health or educational gains elsewhere protects the project from the very comparison public spending requires. B never responded to this, and it remained the strongest unaddressed route to a CON vote.</best_rebuttal>
